mainTopic: Keeping seeds and urine away from a neighbor's wall, and when items placed in a window count as blocking it for טומאה.
overview: The גמרא first questions whether seeds harm a wall because their roots spread sideways, and רבי חגא explains that planting loosens the soil instead. Next, רבה בר בר חנה allows urinating beside a friend's wall, based on a פסוק. Two challenges are answered by saying those sources mean urine poured from a container. But a ברייתא that clearly forbids urinating near a wall refutes him, and the גמרא reads his פסוק as talking about a dog. Then שמואל teaches that a thin wafer placed in a window does not make the window smaller for the laws of טומאה, because the owner does not give it up for good. The גמרא defends this rule against a משנה about straw and dried figs in a window, explaining that those items are useless (rotten, thorny, wet straw and wormy figs). Finally the גמרא starts asking how the barrel of figs was positioned, and that discussion continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Do roots really spread sideways?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא attacks the idea that seeds damage a wall because their roots spread sideways. It cites the law of a bent-down vine, where sowing at the sides is allowed.
steps.simpleTranslation: Do roots really spread to the sides?! We learned that if someone bends a vine branch into the ground and it is covered by less than three טפחים of earth, he may not plant seeds above it. A ברייתא adds that he may plant on either side of it. So roots do not spread sideways.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is challenging the reason it had given for keeping seeds away from a neighbor's wall, namely that their roots spread sideways.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the laws of כלאים, seeds may not go right on top of a buried vine, but they may go next to it. If roots spread sideways, the seeds at the side would mix with the vine and be forbidden. Since they are allowed, roots must grow down and not sideways, so roots cannot be the reason seeds harm a wall.

keyTerms.meaning: they take root, the roots spread
one who bends a vine branch into the ground so it roots as a new vine
and a ברייתא was taught about it

phrases.english: Do they really take root to the sides?!
But didn't we learn:
One who bends a grapevine into the ground,

phrases.aramaic: אִם אֵין עַל גַּבָּהּ עָפָר שְׁלֹשָׁה טְפָחִים –
phrases.english: if there are not three handbreadths of earth on top of it,
he may not plant seed above it;
and it was taught about it:

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל זוֹרֵעַ אֶת הַצְּדָדִין אֵילָךְ וְאֵילָךְ.
phrases.english: but he may sow the sides, on this side and that side.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the discussion of why seeds must be kept away from the wall, before this section.
steps.kashyaTarget: The assumption that seeds harm a wall because their roots spread sideways.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The כלאים ruling allows sowing beside a buried vine, which shows that roots do not spread sideways.

steps.title: The real damage: loosened soil
steps.stepSummary: רבי חגא in the name of רבי יוסי explains that seeds harm a wall because planting breaks up the ground and loosens the soil, not because of roots.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חגא said in the name of רבי יוסי: the reason is that sowing breaks up the ground and raises loose earth, and this weakens the wall's foundation.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a new reason for keeping seeds away from the wall, which avoids the challenge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The distance rule stays the same, but the reason changes. The harm comes from the digging and loose soil that planting causes near the wall, not from roots. So the כלאים source does not contradict the rule.

keyTerms.meaning: an אמורא who quotes רבי יוסי
they break up and hollow out the ground

steps.whatToRemember: Seeds are kept three טפחים from a wall because planting loosens the soil, not because roots spread sideways.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי חַגָּא בְּשֵׁם רַבִּי יוֹסֵי:
phrases.english: Rabbi Ḥagga said in the name of Rabbi Yosei:
Because they break up the ground
and raise up loose earth.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי חַגָּא בְּשֵׁם רַבִּי יוֹסֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 1 by giving a different reason for the rule.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Changes the reason for the rule
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Seeds are kept away because their roots spread sideways into the wall.
steps.terutzMaskana: Seeds are kept away because planting loosens the soil and weakens the wall.

steps.title: The משנה about urine near a wall
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next line of the משנה: urine must be kept three טפחים from a neighbor's wall.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: and urine must be kept three טפחים from the wall, and so on.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is quoting a new line from the משנה to set up the next discussion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the starting point for a new topic. The משנה says urine harms a wall, so it must be kept away. The next steps ask exactly what kind of urine this means.

phrases.english: And urine from the wall —
three handbreadths, etc.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to the next clause of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Urine must be kept three טפחים from a neighbor's wall.

steps.title: Urinating next to a friend's wall is allowed
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר בר חנה rules that a person may urinate next to a friend's wall. He proves it from a פסוק that calls males 'one who urinates against a wall.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר בר חנה said: a person may urinate beside his friend's wall, as the פסוק says: 'I will cut off from אחאב every one who urinates against a wall, and the shut-up and the free in Israel.'
steps.whatsHappening: An אמורא gives a ruling that seems more lenient than the משנה, and he supports it with a פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק uses 'one who urinates against a wall' as a way of saying 'every male.' That shows this was a normal thing people did. So רבה בר בר חנה says it is permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: one who urinates against a wall, meaning a male

phrases.english: Rabba bar bar Ḥana said:
It is permitted for a person to urinate
beside his friend's wall,
as it is written:
"And I will cut off from Ahab every one who urinates against a wall,
and the one shut up and the one left free in Israel."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה: מוּתָּר לָאָדָם לְהַשְׁתִּין מַיִם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a ruling about the משנה's case of urine.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person may urinate next to a friend's wall.

steps.title: Challenge from the משנה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבה בר בר חנה from the משנה, which requires urine to be kept three טפחים from the wall.
steps.simpleTranslation: But we learned in the משנה: urine must be kept three טפחים from the wall!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבה בר בר חנה's ruling, because it seems to contradict the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה requires a distance for urine, but רבה בר בר חנה allows urinating right next to the wall. Both cannot be true unless they are talking about different cases.

phrases.english: But we learned:
And urine from the wall —
three handbreadths!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ruling of step 4 using the משנה from step 3.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה בר בר חנה's ruling that one may urinate next to a friend's wall.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה clearly requires a three-טפחים distance for urine.

steps.title: The משנה means poured urine
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the משנה is talking about urine poured out from a container, not urinating directly.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, the משנה is talking about pouring urine out.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by narrowing the case of the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה's distance rule applies to urine poured out of a container. רבה בר בר חנה's permission applies to a person urinating directly. So the two do not conflict.
steps.confusionAlert: The משנה's rule is not cancelled. It still applies, but only to urine poured from a container.

phrases.english: There, it is about pouring.
phrases.notes: He means urine poured out of a pot, not urine passed directly from the body.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 5.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the source to a specific case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה forbids all urine near a wall, including urinating directly.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה is only talking about urine poured from a container.

steps.title: Challenge from a ברייתא about pouring water
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא: a person may not pour water beside a friend's wall unless he keeps it three טפחים away.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: a person may not pour water beside his friend's wall unless he keeps it three טפחים away from it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second source to challenge רבה בר בר חנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If even pouring water needs a distance, it seems that urinating should certainly need one too. So this ברייתא seems to contradict רבה בר בר חנה's permission.

keyTerms.meaning: come and hear (a source is brought)

phrases.english: Come and hear:
A person may not pour water
beside his friend's wall —

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן הִרְחִיק מִמֶּנּוּ שְׁלֹשָׁה טְפָחִים!
phrases.english: unless he keeps it three handbreadths away from it!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second challenge to רבה בר בר חנה, from a ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה בר בר חנה's permission to urinate next to a friend's wall.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא forbids pouring water near the wall, so urinating there should also be forbidden.

steps.title: The ברייתא also means pouring
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the ברייתא too is talking about pouring, so it does not contradict רבה בר בר חנה.
steps.simpleTranslation: There too, it is talking about pouring.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the same answer as before: this source is also about pouring, not urinating directly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא again says the source is about pouring from a container, not about urinating directly. For now, רבה בר בר חנה's ruling survives this challenge. The next step brings a ברייתא that cannot be explained this way.

phrases.english: There too, it is about pouring.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 7 using the same distinction as step 6.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the source to a specific case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא's ban on pouring would also forbid urinating near the wall.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא only deals with pouring, so urinating directly stays permitted.

steps.title: A ברייתא that clearly says 'urinate'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא forbidding a person to urinate within three טפחים of a friend's brick wall, with less distance for stone and none for hard rock.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: A person may not urinate next to his friend's wall unless he keeps three טפחים away. When is this said? For a brick wall. But for a stone wall, he must keep far enough not to cause damage. How far is that? One טפח. And next to hard rock, it is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבה בר בר חנה again, this time with a ברייתא that clearly talks about urinating directly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier answers said the sources were talking about pouring from a container. This ברייתא uses the word 'urinate' and gives different distances for different wall materials, so the 'pouring' answer cannot work here. The idea is that urine damages the wall, so the softer the material, the more distance is needed.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear: the גמרא is bringing a source
In what case is this said? (introduces a limit on the rule)

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the 'pouring' answer from steps 6 and 8 can save רבה בר בר חנה here. This ברייתא clearly says 'urinate' (לֹא יַשְׁתִּין), and that is why it works as a real challenge.

phrases.aramaic: תָּא שְׁמַע: לֹא יַשְׁתִּין אָדָם מַיִם
phrases.english: Come and hear: A person may not urinate
next to the wall of his friend

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן הִרְחִיק מִמֶּנּוּ שְׁלֹשָׁה טְפָחִים.
phrases.english: unless he distanced himself from it three handbreadths.
In what case is this said?
With a brick wall,
but with a stone wall,
he keeps enough distance so that he will not cause damage.
And how much is that? One handbreadth.
And next to hard rock, it is permitted.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: לֹא יַשְׁתִּין אָדָם מַיִם בְּצַד כּוֹתְלוֹ שֶׁל חֲבֵירוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third challenge. It closes off the 'pouring' answer that worked in steps 6 and 8.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה בר בר חנה's ruling that one may urinate right next to a friend's wall
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא explicitly forbids urinating (not pouring) near a wall, and gives distances by wall type, so it directly contradicts the ruling.

steps.title: רבה בר בר חנה is refuted
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא declares that רבה בר בר חנה's ruling has been refuted.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is a refutation of רבה בר בר חנה; it is a refutation.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא concludes that this ברייתא disproves רבה בר בר חנה's ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since no answer can be given for the ברייתא, his ruling is rejected. The הלכה follows the ברייתא: keep a distance from a friend's wall when urinating.

keyTerms.meaning: A conclusive refutation: the opinion is rejected

steps.whatToRemember: The הלכה is that one must keep away from a friend's wall when urinating: three טפחים for brick, one טפח for stone, and no distance needed next to hard rock.

phrases.english: The refutation of Rabba bar bar Ḥana,
is a conclusive refutation.

steps.triggerLanguage: תְּיוּבְתָּא דְּרַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה, תְּיוּבְתָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the result of the challenge in step 9.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: רבה בר בר חנה's lenient ruling is rejected; a person must keep a distance from a friend's wall.

steps.title: But he brought a פסוק
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how רבה בר בר חנה can be refuted when he based his ruling on a פסוק.
steps.simpleTranslation: But רבה בר בר חנה quoted a פסוק!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks how the ruling can be rejected when it was proven from a פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 4, he showed that the פסוק calls males 'one who urinates against a wall,' which seemed to show this was normal and allowed. A ברייתא cannot simply go against a פסוק, so the פסוק needs to be explained.

phrases.english: But Rabba bar bar Ḥana
stated a verse!
phrases.notes: This is the פסוק from step 4 about 'one who urinates against a wall.'

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה קְרָא קָאָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the refutation by pointing back to רבה בר בר חנה's proof from a פסוק.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ruling rests on a פסוק, and a ברייתא should not be able to override a פסוק.

steps.title: The פסוק is talking about a dog
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that the פסוק means 'even a creature that urinates against walls, a dog, I will not leave,' so it says nothing about people.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, this is what it means: 'I will not leave even something whose way is to urinate against a wall.' And what is that? A dog.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the פסוק is not describing people at all; it is describing a dog.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה בר בר חנה read the phrase as a name for men. The גמרא reads it as 'even a dog,' meaning total destruction of the household. With this reading, the פסוק gives no proof that people may urinate against a wall, and the refutation stands.

keyTerms.meaning: There, this is what it means
I will leave (here: I will not leave)

phrases.english: There, this is what it is saying:
Even something whose way is to urinate against a wall
I will not leave him,
phrases.notes: In the פסוק, these words are said about wiping out a king's household, so not even a dog would be left.

phrases.english: And what is that? A dog.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 11 by reading the פסוק differently.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Re-reading the source: the פסוק refers to a dog, not to people
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The פסוק seemed to call men 'those who urinate against a wall,' as if this were normal and allowed.
steps.terutzMaskana: The פסוק means even a dog will not be left, so it proves nothing about people, and the ברייתא stands.

steps.title: שמואל: a thin wafer does not make a window smaller
steps.stepSummary: רבי טובי בר קיסנא quotes שמואל: placing a thin wafer in a window does not reduce the window's size.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי טובי בר קיסנא said in the name of שמואל: A thin wafer does not make a window smaller.
steps.whatsHappening: A new topic begins. שמואל teaches that a thin wafer sitting in a window does not count as blocking part of it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The size of a window between two rooms can matter in הלכה, for example whether טומאה from a dead body passes from one room to the next. שמואל rules that a wafer placed there is not treated as part of the wall, so the opening keeps its full size.

keyTerms.meaning: A window or opening in a wall

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי טוֹבִי בַּר קִיסְנָא אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל:
phrases.english: Rabbi Tovi bar Kisna says that Shmuel says:
A wafer does not reduce the size of a window.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי טוֹבִי בַּר קִיסְנָא אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic, unrelated to urinating near walls.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A thin wafer placed in a window does not count as reducing the window's opening.

steps.title: Why mention a thin wafer?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why שמואל spoke about a thin wafer, when even a thick piece of bread does not reduce the window.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why specifically a thin wafer? Even a thick piece also does not reduce it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions שמואל's wording: why pick a thin wafer as his example?
steps.deeperAnalysis: It seems obvious that a thick piece of bread would not reduce the window either. Choosing the wafer might suggest that only a wafer works, and the גמרא wants to know why he chose it.

phrases.english: Why specifically a wafer?
Even a thick piece also does not reduce it!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the example שמואל chose in step 13.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's choice of the word רָקִיק
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If a thick piece also does not reduce the window, naming only a wafer seems to leave out the thick piece, or teach nothing special.

steps.title: Not only thick bread, but even a wafer
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that שמואל is teaching 'not only this, but even that.' Thick bread is obviously kept to eat, but even a wafer, which gets gross, is not given up as part of the wall.
steps.simpleTranslation: He is saying 'it is not needed': There is no need to say this about a thick piece, since it is fit for him to use, he does not give it up. But a thin wafer, which becomes disgusting, I might say he does give it up and it becomes part of the wall. So שמואל teaches us that it does not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains that שמואל picked the harder case on purpose: if even a wafer does not reduce the window, a thick piece certainly does not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Something only reduces a window if the owner 'gives it up' (מְבַטֵּל) and leaves it there for good as part of the building. Thick bread is useful, so he clearly plans to take it back. A thin wafer gets gross, so we might think he gave it up, and שמואל teaches that even so, it is not given up.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not needed to say: a 'not only this, but even that' style
Gives it up, leaving it permanently as part of the building
He teaches us (the new point being taught)

steps.whatToRemember: An item placed in a window only reduces the window if the owner gives it up for good. Even a thin wafer that gets gross is not given up, and thick bread certainly is not.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows a common pattern in the גמרא: a teacher often picks the harder case so the easier case is learned automatically.

phrases.english: He is speaking in the style of 'it is not needed':
It is not needed to say this about a thick piece,

phrases.aramaic: כֵּיוָן דְּאִיחֲזִי לֵיהּ, לָא מְבַטֵּיל לֵיהּ;
phrases.english: since it is fit for him, he does not give it up;
but a wafer, which becomes disgusting,
I might say that he does give it up;
so he teaches us that he does not.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 14 by explaining why שמואל chose the wafer.
steps.terutzResolutionType: 'Not only this, but even that': the harder case was chosen on purpose
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A thin wafer, which becomes disgusting, might be given up by its owner and count as part of the wall, making the window smaller.
steps.terutzMaskana: Even a wafer is not given up, so it does not reduce the window; a thick piece certainly does not.

steps.title: Why not use the simpler reason that food can become impure?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why שמואל needed the 'owner will take it' reason. A wafer can become טמא, and anything that can become טמא never blocks טומאה anyway.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why didn't שמואל just say the wafer doesn't block because it can become impure? There is a rule that anything that can become impure does not block impurity.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is challenging the reason given for שמואל's rule. It points out that a different, simpler reason seems to be available.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is a known rule that something which can itself become טמא cannot act as a barrier against טומאה. A wafer is food, and food can become טמא. So the wafer should not block for that reason alone, without needing to talk about whether the owner will remove it.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Let him derive it' from a different, simpler source or reason

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up two different ideas. One is whether the item itself can become impure. The other is whether it blocks impurity from spreading through the window.

phrases.english: But let him derive it
phrases.notes: 'Him' is שמואל, and 'it' is his rule that the wafer doesn't make the window smaller.

phrases.aramaic: דְּהָוֵה לֵיהּ דָּבָר שֶׁהוּא מְקַבֵּל טוּמְאָה,
phrases.english: from the fact that it is an item that can become impure,
and any item that can become impure
does not block against impurity!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reasoning given in Step 15 by suggesting a simpler reason that makes it unnecessary.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reason given for שמואל's ruling (that the owner keeps the wafer to remove it).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A wafer can become טמא, and anything that can become טמא never blocks. So the 'owner will remove it' reason seems unnecessary.

steps.title: The wafer was kneaded with fruit juice
steps.stepSummary: The case is a wafer kneaded with fruit juice. Such a wafer cannot become טמא, so the simpler reason doesn't work and שמואל needed his own reason.
steps.simpleTranslation: The wafer was kneaded with fruit juice.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by narrowing the case to a wafer that cannot become impure. That way the simpler reason no longer applies.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Food can only become טמא after certain liquids have touched it, and fruit juice is not one of them. A wafer made with fruit juice therefore cannot become impure. Without שמואל's teaching, we might think such a wafer does block, so his reason is still needed.

keyTerms.meaning: Thin wafer (the item discussed since שמואל's statement)

phrases.english: Where it was kneaded with fruit juice.
phrases.notes: Fruit juice doesn't make food able to become impure, so this wafer can't become impure at all.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 16 by setting the case where the simpler reason does not apply.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any wafer can become impure, so שמואל's reason was unnecessary.
steps.terutzMaskana: שמואל speaks of a wafer that cannot become impure, so only his reason explains why it doesn't block.

steps.title: Challenge from the משנה about straw and figs in a window
steps.stepSummary: A משנה says a basket of straw or a barrel of dried figs in a window blocks טומאה if the contents could stand on their own. But straw is useful as animal food, so by שמואל's logic it should not count.
steps.simpleTranslation: A basket full of straw or a barrel full of dried figs placed in a window is judged this way. If the straw or figs could stand by themselves once the container is removed, they block. If not, they don't block. But straw is good for feeding one's animal!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a משנה that seems to contradict שמואל. Useful things in a window are counted as blocking, even though the owner might take them away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל's idea is that something the owner plans to use is not treated as part of the wall. Straw can feed animals, so the owner will likely take it. Yet the משנה says it does block, which goes against שמואל.

keyTerms.meaning: 'They challenged': introduces a challenge from an earlier source

phrases.english: They raised a challenge: a basket full of straw,
phrases.notes: This is a משנה in אהלות 6:2.

phrases.english: or a barrel full of dried figs,
that are placed in a window – we look:
in any case where, if they were removed,
phrases.notes: 'They' means the basket and the barrel, not what's inside them.

phrases.aramaic: וִיכוֹלִין תֶּבֶן וּגְרוֹגְרוֹת לַעֲמוֹד בִּפְנֵי עַצְמָן –
phrases.english: the straw and figs could stand on their own –
they block; and if not – they do not block.
But straw is fit for his animal!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new challenge to שמואל's rule, this time from a משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's rule that usable items in a window do not count as part of the wall.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה treats straw as blocking even though it is useful as animal food, which contradicts שמואל's logic.

steps.title: The straw is rotten
steps.stepSummary: The משנה speaks of rotten straw, which animals won't eat.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is talking about rotten straw.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the straw in the משנה is rotten. It is not animal food, so the owner won't take it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the straw has no use, the owner leaves it in place, and it becomes part of the wall. So the משנה fits with שמואל.

phrases.english: With rotten straw.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 18 by narrowing the case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The straw is good animal food, so the owner would take it.
steps.terutzMaskana: The straw is rotten and useless for animals, so it stays and blocks.

steps.title: Rotten straw is still good for clay
steps.stepSummary: Even rotten straw can be mixed into clay for bricks, so the owner might still take it.
steps.simpleTranslation: But it is fit for clay!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back: rotten straw still has a use.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Straw was mixed into clay to make bricks. If it has that use, the owner may still remove it, and the problem returns.

keyTerms.meaning: Clay or mud, mixed with straw for bricks

phrases.english: It is fit for clay!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of Step 19.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that the straw is rotten.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Rotten straw is still useful for brick-making clay, so the owner may remove it.

steps.title: The straw has thorns in it
steps.stepSummary: The straw has thorns, so it cannot be used for clay.
steps.simpleTranslation: It has thorns in it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that this straw is full of thorns, so nobody would knead it into clay.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Thorny straw would hurt the hands of whoever kneads the clay. So that use is ruled out too, and the straw stays useless.

phrases.english: That has thorns in it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 20 by adding a detail to the case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The straw could be used for clay.
steps.terutzMaskana: The straw is thorny and not usable for clay.

steps.title: The straw could still be used to start a fire
steps.stepSummary: Even thorny, rotten straw can be burned for fuel.
steps.simpleTranslation: But it is fit for burning!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finds yet another use for the straw: fuel.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the straw can be burned, the owner may take it to light a fire. Then it would not count as part of the wall.

phrases.english: It is fit for burning!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of Step 21.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that the straw is rotten and thorny.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Such straw is still usable as fuel, so the owner may remove it.

steps.title: The straw is wet
steps.stepSummary: The straw is wet, so it won't burn.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is wet straw.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the straw is damp, so it can't be used to light a fire.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Wet straw doesn't catch fire, which removes the fuel use. The straw is still useless and stays in the window.

phrases.english: With wet straw.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 22 by adding that the straw is wet.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The straw could be used as fuel.
steps.terutzMaskana: The straw is wet and won't burn.

steps.title: Wet straw still burns in a big fire
steps.stepSummary: In a large fire, even wet straw dries out and burns, so it is still useful.
steps.simpleTranslation: But it is fit for a big fire!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes once more: a big fire can burn even wet straw.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A large, hot fire dries wet straw and burns it. So the straw still has some use, and the owner might take it.

phrases.english: It is fit for a big fire!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of Step 23.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that the straw is wet.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A large fire would burn even wet straw, so the straw is still usable.

steps.title: Big fires are not common
steps.stepSummary: People rarely make big fires, so the owner won't plan to take the straw.
steps.simpleTranslation: A big fire is not common.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that big fires are rare. A use that seldom comes up doesn't make the owner keep the straw to remove it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We judge by normal behavior. A rare use doesn't count, so the straw is treated as useless and becomes part of the wall, just as the משנה says.
steps.whatToRemember: The straw in the משנה is rotten, thorny, and wet. It has no normal use, so it stays in the window as part of the wall and blocks. This fits שמואל's rule.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets a general idea: a rare, unusual use does not stop something from being treated as abandoned in place.

phrases.english: A big fire is not common.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 24 and closes the discussion of the straw.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any possible use, even a rare one, means the owner may take it.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only common uses count, and a big fire is uncommon.

steps.title: Dried figs are surely edible
steps.stepSummary: The משנה also says dried figs block. But figs are food, and the owner will surely take them.
steps.simpleTranslation: But dried figs are fit for him to eat!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns to the second item in the משנה, the figs, and asks the same question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Figs are good food, so by שמואל's logic the owner will remove them. They shouldn't count as part of the wall, yet the משנה says they block.

keyTerms.meaning: They are fit for him (to eat)

phrases.english: Dried figs – but they are fit for him!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the משנה of Step 18 to challenge its second case, the figs.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's ruling that dried figs in a window block.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Figs are edible, so the owner would remove them. By שמואל's logic they shouldn't count as part of the wall.

steps.title: שמואל: the figs are wormy
steps.stepSummary: שמואל explains that the figs in the משנה became infested with worms, so nobody will eat them.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל said: it is talking about figs that became wormy.
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל answers that the figs are worm-infested and useless, so the owner leaves them in place.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Wormy figs are not eaten, so they are like the useless straw. They become part of the wall and block, which fits שמואל's rule.

keyTerms.meaning: The אמורא whose rule is being defended

phrases.english: Shmuel said:
Where they became wormy.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 26 by narrowing the case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The figs are good to eat, so the owner would take them.
steps.terutzMaskana: The figs are wormy and useless, so they stay and block.

steps.title: רבה בר אבוה teaches the same
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא taught by רבה בר אבוה also explains the figs as wormy, which supports שמואל.
steps.simpleTranslation: And so רבה בר אבוה taught: it is talking about figs that became wormy.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא supports שמואל's answer by showing that a ברייתא taught the same explanation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל's answer is not just a convenient guess. An earlier teaching taught by רבה בר אבוה says the same, so the משנה really does fit with שמואל's rule.

keyTerms.meaning: 'And so it was taught': brings a supporting teaching
The אמורא who taught this ברייתא
A teaching from the time of the משנה that is not in the משנה itself

steps.whatToRemember: Both the straw and the figs in the משנה are useless, so they block. This keeps שמואל's rule: useful items in a window are expected to be removed and do not count as part of the wall.

phrases.english: And so Rabba bar Avuh taught:
Where they became wormy.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the answer of Step 27 with a ברייתא.
steps.raayaObject: שמואל's explanation that the figs in the משנה were wormy.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא taught by רבה בר אבוה giving the same explanation.

steps.title: How exactly was the barrel positioned?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the case of the barrel of figs looks like, and starts with the option that its opening faced outward.
steps.simpleTranslation: This barrel, what is the case? If its opening faced outward...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks how the barrel holding the dried figs was set up, and starts testing the first possibility. This is a setup line, and the גמרא finishes the thought on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now the discussion was about the figs themselves being wormy. Now the focus moves to the barrel they sit in, and which way its opening faced. The first option is an opening facing outward, away from the source of the טומאה.

keyTerms.meaning: A barrel, here the one holding the dried figs
What does it look like? What exactly is the case?

steps.confusionAlert: This line is not finished. 'If its opening faced outward' is only the first half of a sentence. The גמרא's answer about this option comes on the next amud.

phrases.english: This barrel, what are its circumstances?
If its opening faced outward,
phrases.notes: Outward means facing away from the source of the טומאה.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַאי חָבִית, הֵיכִי דָּמְיָא? אִי דְּפוּמָּא לְבַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After settling that the figs were wormy, the גמרא now looks at how the barrel holding them was set up.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which way the opening of the barrel of figs faced, and how that affects whether it blocks the טומאה.
